subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: Calculate the torque of a force about an axis
An unbalanced torque produces angular acceleration
Describe rotation with angular displacement, velocity and acceleration
Use the equations for uniform angular acceleration
Moment of inertia depends on how mass is spread about the axis
Moment of inertia of point masses
Angular momentum of a rotating body
Angular momentum is conserved without an external torque
Angular impulse equals the change in angular momentum
Rotational kinetic energy and rolling bodies

questions.q: A rigid body is free to turn about a fixed axis. One of the forces acting on it lies in a plane perpendicular to the axis. Under which condition is the torque of this force about the axis zero?
options: It acts perpendicular to the line from the axis to where it acts.
The body remains at rest while this force acts on it.
An equal force acts on the other side, at the same distance.
Its line of action passes through the axis of rotation.
optionWhy: A student who uses cos θ in the torque equation thinks a perpendicular force gives zero torque. In fact θ = 90° gives sin θ = 1, the maximum torque for that force and distance.

A student who thinks a torque exists only when the body turns picks this. A body can stay at rest while this force exerts a torque, if other torques balance it; the force's own torque is still Fr sin θ.

A student who thinks a balancing force removes this force's own torque picks this. An equal force on the other side at the same distance can make the RESULTANT torque zero, but the torque of this force is still Fr sin θ, which other forces do not change.
τ = Fr sin θ. If the line of action passes through the axis, θ = 0° or 180°, so sin θ = 0; equivalently the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action is zero.
questions.explain: τ = Fr sin θ. If the line of action passes through the axis, θ = 0° or 180°, so sin θ = 0; equivalently the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action is zero.

questions.q: A rigid body is in rotational equilibrium. Which statement about the body must be true?
options: The body is not rotating about any axis.
The forces on each side of its axis are equal.
The resultant torque acting on the body is zero.
The resultant force acting on the body is zero.
optionWhy: A student who equates equilibrium with being at rest picks this. A body with zero resultant torque has constant angular velocity, which need not be zero: a wheel spinning steadily on a frictionless axle is in rotational equilibrium.
A student who judges balance by equal forces picks this. The torques must balance, and a small force far from the axis can balance a large force close to it.
Rotational equilibrium is defined by zero resultant torque, so there is no angular acceleration. The body may be at rest or rotating at a constant angular speed.

A student who merges the two equilibrium conditions picks this. Zero resultant torque does not require zero resultant force: a box pulled along by a force through its centre of mass accelerates without rotating.
questions.explain: Rotational equilibrium is defined by zero resultant torque, so there is no angular acceleration. The body may be at rest or rotating at a constant angular speed.

questions.q: A wheel is mounted on a frictionless axle. Starting from rest, a constant resultant torque acts on it for a few seconds and is then removed. How does the wheel move after the torque is removed?
options: It keeps rotating at a constant angular speed.
It slows down steadily and then stops rotating.
Its angular speed rises until the torque is used up.
It stops, as its angular acceleration is now zero.
optionWhy: With no resultant torque there is no angular acceleration (α = τ/I = 0), so the wheel keeps the angular speed it had when the torque was removed. This is the rotational form of Newton's first law.
A student who thinks a torque is needed to keep a body rotating picks this. Real wheels slow because friction exerts a torque; on a frictionless axle nothing changes the angular speed.
A student who pictures the torque as stored in the wheel picks this. Angular acceleration exists only while a torque acts: once the torque is removed, α = 0 at once.
A student who confuses zero angular acceleration with zero angular velocity picks this. α = 0 means the angular velocity is constant, at the non-zero value reached when the torque stopped.
questions.explain: With no resultant torque there is no angular acceleration (α = τ/I = 0), so the wheel keeps the angular speed it had when the torque was removed. This is the rotational form of Newton's first law.

questions.q: A rigid disc rotates at a steady rate about a fixed axis through its centre. Point P on the disc is 0.10 m from the axis and point Q is 0.20 m from the axis. How do the motions of P and Q compare?
options: Q has twice the angular velocity and twice the linear speed.
Both have the same angular velocity and the same linear speed.
Same angular velocity; Q has twice the linear speed of P.
Q has half the angular velocity of P, because ω = v/r.
optionWhy: A student who does not separate angular from linear speed thinks the faster-moving point Q must also rotate faster. Both points complete a revolution in the same time, so their angular velocities are equal.
A student who thinks every part of a rigid body moves at the same speed picks this. In rotation Q travels round a circle twice as large in the same time, so its linear speed v = ωr is twice P's.
Every point of a rigid body turns through the same angle in the same time, so P and Q share one angular velocity. Linear speed v = ωr, so Q, at twice the distance, has twice the linear speed.
A student who reads ω = v/r with v held constant picks this. On a rigid body ω is the same everywhere; it is v that is proportional to r.
questions.explain: Every point of a rigid body turns through the same angle in the same time, so P and Q share one angular velocity. Linear speed v = ωr, so Q, at twice the distance, has twice the linear speed.

questions.q: A flywheel rotating at 1500 revolutions per minute is brought to rest with uniform angular deceleration in 20 s. Through what angular displacement does it turn while stopping? (1 revolution = 2π rad.)
optionWhy: A student who treats the angular speed as constant uses Δθ = ω_i t = 157 × 20 = 3.14 × 10³ rad. The flywheel slows uniformly, so its average angular speed is half the initial value.
A student who uses 1500 rev min⁻¹ as if it were 1500 rad s⁻¹ gets (1500/2) × 20 = 1.50 × 10⁴ rad. The rate must first be converted: 1500 × 2π/60 = 157 rad s⁻¹.

A student who takes the deceleration as positive uses Δθ = ω_i t + ½αt² with α = +7.85 rad s⁻², getting 3142 + 1571 = 4.71 × 10³ rad. For a slowing wheel α is negative, which gives 3142 − 1571 = 1.57 × 10³ rad.
questions.working: ω_i = 1500 rev min⁻¹ × 2π rad/rev ÷ 60 s min⁻¹ = 157.1 rad s⁻¹; ω_f = 0. Δθ = ((ω_f + ω_i)/2)t = (157.1 rad s⁻¹/2)(20 s) = 1571 rad ≈ 1.57 × 10³ rad. (Check: α = −157.1/20 = −7.85 rad s⁻²; Δθ = ω_i t + ½αt² = 3142 − 1571 = 1571 rad.)

questions.q: A wheel starts from rest and turns with a uniform angular acceleration of 3.0 rad s⁻². What is its angular speed at the moment it completes 8.0 revolutions?
options: 6.93 rad s⁻¹
12.3 rad s⁻¹
8.68 rad s⁻¹
17.4 rad s⁻¹
optionWhy: A student who uses 8.0 revolutions as 8.0 rad gets ω_f = √(2 × 3.0 × 8.0) = 6.93 rad s⁻¹. Each revolution is 2π rad, so Δθ = 50.3 rad.
A student who drops the factor 2 uses ω_f² = αΔθ = 3.0 × 50.3 and gets 12.3 rad s⁻¹. The equation is ω_f² = ω_i² + 2αΔθ.

A student who finds the time (t = √(2Δθ/α) = 5.79 s) and then divides the angle by the time gets 50.3/5.79 = 8.68 rad s⁻¹. That is the average angular speed; starting from rest, the final value is twice as large.
Δθ = 8.0 × 2π = 50.3 rad. ω_f² = ω_i² + 2αΔθ = 0 + 2 × 3.0 × 50.3 = 302 rad² s⁻², so ω_f = 17.4 rad s⁻¹.
questions.explain: Δθ = 8.0 × 2π = 50.3 rad. ω_f² = ω_i² + 2αΔθ = 0 + 2 × 3.0 × 50.3 = 302 rad² s⁻², so ω_f = 17.4 rad s⁻¹.
questions.working: Δθ = 8.0 rev × 2π rad/rev = 50.27 rad. ω_f² = ω_i² + 2αΔθ = 0 + 2(3.0 rad s⁻²)(50.27 rad) = 301.6 rad² s⁻². ω_f = 17.4 rad s⁻¹.

questions.q: A thin hoop and a uniform solid disc have the same mass and the same radius. Each rotates about an axis through its centre, perpendicular to its plane. Which has the greater moment of inertia about this axis?
options: Neither, because bodies of equal mass have equal moments of inertia.
The hoop, as all its mass is at the maximum distance from the axis.
The disc, since its mass is spread out over its whole area.
Whichever of the two is rotating at the greater angular speed.
optionWhy: A student who treats moment of inertia as the same thing as mass picks this. Moment of inertia depends on the distribution of mass about the axis, not just the amount.
Moment of inertia depends on how far the mass is from the axis. All of the hoop's mass is at distance R (I = MR²); much of the disc's mass is nearer the axis (I = ½MR²).

A student who equates 'spread out' with 'covering more area' picks this. What matters is distance from the axis: the disc has much of its mass close to the centre, so its moment of inertia is smaller.
A student who thinks moment of inertia depends on how fast a body spins picks this. For a rigid body about a given axis, I depends only on the mass distribution.
questions.explain: Moment of inertia depends on how far the mass is from the axis. All of the hoop's mass is at distance R (I = MR²); much of the disc's mass is nearer the axis (I = ½MR²).

questions.q: A system of small masses rotates about a fixed axis. Which single change doubles its moment of inertia about that axis?
options: Doubling each mass, with all distances kept unchanged
Doubling each distance from the axis, with all masses unchanged
Doubling the angular speed at which the system is rotating
Adding a mass equal to the total mass, placed on the axis
optionWhy: I = Σmr². Doubling every m with every r unchanged doubles every term, so I doubles.
A student who thinks I is proportional to r picks this. Because I = Σmr², doubling every distance multiplies I by 2² = 4.
A student who thinks moment of inertia depends on how fast the body spins picks this. I depends only on the masses and their distances from the axis; doubling ω doubles L, not I.
A student who treats moment of inertia as mass alone picks this. A mass on the axis has r = 0, so it adds nothing to Σmr²; I is unchanged.
questions.explain: I = Σmr². Doubling every m with every r unchanged doubles every term, so I doubles.

questions.q: A flywheel of moment of inertia 0.50 kg m² is driven by a belt that exerts a tangential force of 40 N on its rim, 0.30 m from the axis. A frictional torque of 2.0 N m acts at the bearing, opposing the rotation. What is the angular acceleration of the flywheel?
options: 24 rad s⁻²
20 rad s⁻²
28 rad s⁻²
76 rad s⁻²
optionWhy: A student who uses the driving torque alone gets 12/0.50 = 24 rad s⁻². τ in τ = Iα is the resultant torque, so the 2.0 N m friction torque must be subtracted.
Driving torque = Fr = 40 × 0.30 = 12 N m. The friction torque has the opposite sense, so the resultant torque is 12 − 2.0 = 10 N m, and α = τ/I = 10/0.50 = 20 rad s⁻².
A student who adds the torques regardless of sense gets (12 + 2.0)/0.50 = 28 rad s⁻². The friction torque opposes the rotation, so it reduces the resultant torque.
A student who uses the belt force as if it were a torque gets (40 − 2.0)/0.50 = 76 rad s⁻². The force must be multiplied by its distance from the axis: τ = 40 × 0.30 = 12 N m.
questions.explain: Driving torque = Fr = 40 × 0.30 = 12 N m. The friction torque has the opposite sense, so the resultant torque is 12 − 2.0 = 10 N m, and α = τ/I = 10/0.50 = 20 rad s⁻².
questions.working: Driving torque τ₁ = Fr = (40 N)(0.30 m) = 12 N m. Friction torque 2.0 N m in the opposite sense. Resultant τ = 12 − 2.0 = 10 N m. α = τ/I = (10 N m)/(0.50 kg m²) = 20 rad s⁻².

questions.q: A rigid body rotates about a fixed axis. Its angular momentum about that axis is determined by which quantities?
options: Its mass and angular speed, however the mass is arranged
Its mass and the linear speed of its centre of mass
The resultant torque that is acting on it at that instant
Its moment of inertia about that axis and its angular speed
optionWhy: A student who treats moment of inertia as mass alone picks this. Two bodies of the same mass spinning at the same rate have different angular momenta if their mass is at different distances from the axis.
A student who confuses angular momentum with linear momentum mv picks this. A wheel spinning on a fixed axle has a stationary centre of mass but a non-zero angular momentum Iω.
A student who links the amount of rotation to the torque currently acting picks this. Torque sets the RATE of change of angular momentum; a freely spinning body with no torque still has L = Iω.
L = Iω. The moment of inertia carries the information about the mass and how it is distributed about the axis; the angular speed says how fast the body turns.
questions.explain: L = Iω. The moment of inertia carries the information about the mass and how it is distributed about the axis; the angular speed says how fast the body turns.

questions.q: A turntable of moment of inertia 0.020 kg m² rotates freely at 3.0 rad s⁻¹ on a frictionless bearing. A disc of moment of inertia 0.010 kg m², not rotating, is dropped onto it so that both share the same axis. Friction between them soon makes them rotate together. What is their common angular speed?
options: 2.0 rad s⁻¹
3.0 rad s⁻¹
1.5 rad s⁻¹
2.4 rad s⁻¹
optionWhy: No external torque acts about the axis, so angular momentum is conserved: 0.020 × 3.0 = (0.020 + 0.010)ω, giving ω = 0.060/0.030 = 2.0 rad s⁻¹.
A student who thinks the angular speed is conserved when there is no external torque picks this. The moment of inertia has increased, so to keep Iω constant the angular speed must fall.
A student who averages the two angular speeds, (3.0 + 0)/2, gets 1.5 rad s⁻¹. The speeds must be weighted by the moments of inertia: the turntable has twice the disc's I.
A student who conserves kinetic energy, ½(0.020)(3.0)² = ½(0.030)ω², gets 2.4 rad s⁻¹. Friction between the discs dissipates energy, so kinetic energy is not conserved; angular momentum is.
questions.explain: No external torque acts about the axis, so angular momentum is conserved: 0.020 × 3.0 = (0.020 + 0.010)ω, giving ω = 0.060/0.030 = 2.0 rad s⁻¹.
questions.working: No external torque about the axis: L conserved. I₁ω₁ + I₂ω₂ = (I₁ + I₂)ω → (0.020)(3.0) + (0.010)(0) = (0.030)ω → ω = 0.060/0.030 = 2.0 rad s⁻¹.

questions.q: A diver leaves a springboard rotating slowly with her body straight. In the air she pulls into a tight tuck and rotates much faster. Air resistance is negligible. Why does her angular speed increase?
options: Her moment of inertia decreases while her angular momentum stays constant.
Pulling in her limbs exerts an external torque on her, which speeds her up.
Her weight exerts a torque about her centre of mass as she falls.
Her angular momentum increases as she falls and her speed increases.
optionWhy: In the air no external torque acts about her centre of mass, so her angular momentum Iω is constant. Tucking brings mass closer to the axis, reducing I, so ω increases.

A student who thinks any increase in angular speed needs an external torque picks this. The forces that pull her limbs in are internal; they cannot change her total angular momentum. The spin rate rises because I falls.

A student who links the fall to the faster spin picks this. Her weight acts at her centre of mass, so it has no torque about that point; it accelerates her centre of mass downward but does not change her spin.

A student who confuses angular momentum with linear momentum picks this. Her linear momentum increases as she falls, but her angular momentum about her centre of mass is constant because no torque acts about it.
questions.explain: In the air no external torque acts about her centre of mass, so her angular momentum Iω is constant. Tucking brings mass closer to the axis, reducing I, so ω increases.

questions.q: A wheel of moment of inertia 0.50 kg m² rotates counter-clockwise at 12 rad s⁻¹. A torque acts on it for 2.0 s, after which the wheel rotates clockwise at 4.0 rad s⁻¹. What is the magnitude of the average torque on the wheel?
options: 2.0 N m
1.0 N m
4.0 N m
8.0 N m
optionWhy: A student who takes the change in angular speed as the larger value minus the smaller gets 0.50 × (12 − 4.0)/2.0 = 2.0 N m. The wheel reverses: with counter-clockwise positive, Δω = (−4.0) − (+12) = −16 rad s⁻¹, so the average torque has magnitude 0.50 × 16/2.0 = 4.0 N m.

A student who takes the change in angular momentum to be the final angular momentum uses 0.50 × 4.0 = 2.0 N m s and gets 1.0 N m. The initial angular momentum must be subtracted: ΔL = L_final − L_initial.
Taking counter-clockwise as positive, ΔL = I(ω_f − ω_i) = 0.50 × (−4.0 − 12) = −8.0 N m s. τ = ΔL/Δt = −8.0/2.0, a torque of 4.0 N m in the clockwise sense.
A student who equates the torque with the angular impulse gives 0.50 × 16 = 8.0 as the torque. 8.0 N m s is the angular impulse; dividing by the 2.0 s gives the average torque, 4.0 N m.
questions.explain: Taking counter-clockwise as positive, ΔL = I(ω_f − ω_i) = 0.50 × (−4.0 − 12) = −8.0 N m s. τ = ΔL/Δt = −8.0/2.0, a torque of 4.0 N m in the clockwise sense.
questions.working: Take counter-clockwise as positive: ω_i = +12 rad s⁻¹, ω_f = −4.0 rad s⁻¹. ΔL = I(ω_f − ω_i) = (0.50 kg m²)(−16 rad s⁻¹) = −8.0 N m s. τ = ΔL/Δt = −8.0/2.0 = −4.0 N m, i.e. 4.0 N m clockwise.

questions.q: A solid cylinder of mass 2.0 kg and radius 0.10 m is released from rest and rolls without slipping down a slope, descending a vertical height of 0.90 m. For the cylinder, I = ½MR². Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and ignore energy dissipation. What is the speed of its centre of mass at the bottom of the slope?
options: 4.2 m s⁻¹
3.4 m s⁻¹
3.0 m s⁻¹
1.7 m s⁻¹
optionWhy: A student who ignores rotational kinetic energy uses Mgh = ½Mv² and gets v = √(2gh) = 4.2 m s⁻¹. That is the speed of a body sliding without friction; a rolling cylinder puts a third of its kinetic energy into rotation.
Mgh = ½Mv² + ½Iω² with ω = v/R and I = ½MR², so Mgh = ½Mv² + ¼Mv² = ¾Mv². v = √(4gh/3) = √(4 × 9.8 × 0.90/3) = 3.4 m s⁻¹.
A student who writes rotational kinetic energy as Iω² (no ½) gets Mgh = ½Mv² + ½Mv², so v = √(gh) = 3.0 m s⁻¹. Rotational kinetic energy is ½Iω² = ¼Mv² here.
A student who does not square R in I = ½MR² gets I = 0.10 and ½Iω² = 5v², so 17.64 = v² + 5v² and v = 1.7 m s⁻¹. With R squared, I = 0.010 kg m² and ½Iω² = 0.50v².
questions.explain: Mgh = ½Mv² + ½Iω² with ω = v/R and I = ½MR², so Mgh = ½Mv² + ¼Mv² = ¾Mv². v = √(4gh/3) = √(4 × 9.8 × 0.90/3) = 3.4 m s⁻¹.
questions.working: E_p lost = Mgh = (2.0 kg)(9.8 m s⁻²)(0.90 m) = 17.64 J. Rolling without slipping: ω = v/R. E_k = ½Mv² + ½(½MR²)(v/R)² = ¾Mv² = 1.5v² (in J, v in m s⁻¹). 1.5v² = 17.64 → v² = 11.76 → v = 3.4 m s⁻¹.
